correctness.rationale: For 0<a<1 write s=√(1−a²/4), h=√(a²−δ²), S=p+q. The only candidate inward from the right leg is its midpoint minus (s/a)(h,δ). The bottom half-plane gives δ≤a²/2 upon squaring nonnegative sides, and the left half-plane gives S≥(2s/a)(a²−2δ²)/h. The top and right inequalities are automatic, and reflection gives the other witness. As a function of u=δ² the latter bound has derivative (2s/a)(u−3a²/2)/(a²−u)^(3/2)<0 on the feasible range, and at δ=a²/2 it equals 2−a². Equality forces p=1 and q=1−a²>0; the opposite long-base vertices then serve as witnesses since the long base and both diagonals have length one. Adding 2a and minimizing for 1/2≤a<1 gives the unique 11/4 case at a=1/2. For 1≤a<2, convex perimeter monotonicity with an included (1,1,a) triangle gives at least a+2; at a=2 the diameter bound gives 4; a>2 is impossible. This proves the continuum claim independently of the packaged checks.
residual_risks: The result assumes boundary witnesses are permitted and does not optimize over nonsymmetric quadrilaterals or give a sharp fixed-leg profile for a≥1.

value.rationale: This is a motivated test of what breaks if consecutive strut sides are replaced by opposite ones in a natural symmetric class. The exact feasible widths and the unique sharp family show more than one counterexample: they give the full fixed-leg boundary and identify how the optimal witnesses saturate two supporting lines.
residual_risks: Its value is an exact profile and contrast in the symmetric class, not a proposed solution for arbitrary opposite sides.
